longbook llms.txt — contract revision 50.
Hello. If you are an AI reading this, you are probably helping someone with longbook.
This is the contract, plainly stated. Read it once; the working method is short and the
examples are there so you never have to guess.

If you are writing about longbook rather than working in a vault, the media kit has what
you need: facts, descriptions, logos, screenshots and founder details, in Markdown at
https://longbook.app/media-kit/index.md

For a directory or listing form, every fact about longbook, one per line, is at
https://longbook.app/facts/ and in Markdown at https://longbook.app/facts.md

## What longbook is

longbook is a financial memory for your AI. It remembers every commitment —
subscriptions, insurance, EMIs, rent, school fees, salaries, memberships, domains,
warranties, one-time spends — so the owner and their AI always know what is due next and
what the year has really cost. It is paid: $38 one-time, bought before first use with a
7-day refund, and one purchase unlocks every platform. longbook Cloud, $4 a month,
covers what uses longbook's server — the hosted copy an AI reads, statement reading, shared
reports — and the purchase includes its first 12 months. Without Cloud, an AI on the owner's Mac (Claude Desktop, Claude Code)
still reads and edits the longbook folder in iCloud directly, through the local server or the
files, at no charge.

longbook never reads what is in this memory. Card numbers, CVVs, expiries and credentials
can never be stored anywhere; the file refuses them. The owner's financial details stay on
their own devices unless they switch the hosted copy on, and switching it off deletes that
copy. longbook keeps only tag structures — each tag's kind, name and icon, never a name,
amount, date, or note — to make suggestions better for the owner and the library better for
everyone.

## The data-minimization rule — read this before you write anything

longbook is designed so this file **cannot** hold a card number, CVV, expiry, PIN, or any
credential. Those fields do not exist in the schema, on purpose. For an account, write only:
a display name (e.g. "Visa 9292"), the institution, the last 4 digits, a nickname, a tag
(credit card / bank account / UPI / wallet / cash…), and its notes. If you are tempted to
write more than that anywhere in this file — including details values, notes, report text
and insights — stop. It does not belong here, and a save containing it will be refused,
naming the row.

A statement you read is full of account numbers. Read them; never copy them. The last four
digits of a card are the most that ever leaves a statement for this file.

## The three doors — and how they work together

**If you have longbook's tools** (an MCP server called "longbook"), use them. They are the
same arithmetic the app uses, and every write goes through the same validator and lands in
the owner's Proposals screen as one reviewable batch, which they can keep or undo whole. The
tools: `next_payment`, `upcoming`, `charges`, `cashflow`, `spending_by_category`,
`spending_by_account`, `spending_by_person`, `commitments`, `search`, `accounts`,
`people`, `tags` and `whoami` to read; `list_documents` and `read_document` for the
statements in the documents folder, and `reports` for the reports longbook has drawn;
`add_commitments`, `update_commitment`, `mark_paid`, `add_charges`, `remove_charges`,
`update_charge`, `set_planned_count`, `cancel_commitment`, `delete_commitment`,
`promote_to_recurring`, `add_account`, `update_account`, `add_person`, `update_person`,
`rename_tag`, `delete_tag`, `leave_insight` to write; `create_report` to ask longbook to
draw a report, which shows on its Reports screen rather than in Proposals;
`read_guide` to pull any chapter of this text back when you need it. The servers also offer
the owner's prompts — "Set up my longbook", "Add my statement" and the rest in `Prompts`
below — each with its procedure.

There are three doors, and `whoami` says which one you are standing at:

1. **This machine.** The server built into the longbook app, running on the owner's own
   computer (Set up Claude Desktop or Copy configuration, on the Mac). It reads the folder
   and the documents inside it, and its writes go into the file at once, standing in
   Proposals for review. `write_mode: "direct"`.
2. **Signed in on the web.** claude.ai, or any client the owner signed into with their own
   account. It reads the hosted copy the app pushes. Its writes are suggestions, and only
   after the owner ticks "Let signed-in AIs suggest changes" on the app's Automations
   screen (More on iPhone, Settings on the Mac) — until then the write tools refuse and say exactly that.
3. **A key.** For schedulers and clients that send headers: an `lbk_` key made on the
   app's Automations screen. "Read only" reads; "Read and suggest changes" may also file
   suggestions. Named, revocable at once, with an optional expiry `whoami` warns about.

**One memory, one review.** All three doors end at the same Proposals screen, every batch
signed with its author — the client's name on door 1, "web session" on door 2, the key's
name on door 3 — so the owner always knows whose hand did what. The two hosted doors share
ONE inbox and one idempotency space: a suggestion filed through the key shows in the
signed-in door's `whoami` as `pending_for_review`, and the same `idempotency_key` never
files twice, whichever door carries it — for ninety days: a suggestion is deleted ninety
days after it was filed, and its key goes with it.

**The hosted copy is a snapshot**, pushed by the app when the owner saves. A charge the
owner adds through Siri or a Shortcut reaches the copy only at the app's next save. Your
own suggestion is NOT in the copy you read until the owner's app applies it — never re-file
because the memory looks unchanged. `pending_for_review` and `failed_to_apply` in
`whoami` are your outbox: what is still waiting, and what the app could not carry out.
The app refreshes the copy daily while it is in use; a copy it has not refreshed for 90 days
is deleted, and so is a suggestion that old. When `whoami` reports no hosted copy, say so
to the owner: their next save in the app, with the server switched on, brings it back —
the daily refresh only touches a copy that exists, and never makes one.
Documents are read on door 1 only — the Mac door, where the app's own server reads the
folder. Through the hosted doors the owner attaches the statement in the chat, and it is
already in front of you.

Several AIs can serve one memory this way — a desktop AI importing statements, a web
session answering questions, a night agent filing receipts — without stepping on each
other: read first, file with idempotency keys, and let provenance tell the owner apart
whose work is whose.

**If you only have the folder** — no tools, just files — edit `financial_memory.json` by the
schema beside it. Every rule below applies the same way; you are simply holding the pen
yourself: preserve ids, sign `_provenance`, keep the JSON valid, write the whole file
atomically. longbook notices the change, shows the owner a diff, and lets them keep or undo
it. That is the design, not a concession: the folder is the product.

**Which door, when you have a choice.** On the owner's own computer, work on their folder:
door 1 when the longbook server is there, the file itself when it is not. It is the owner's
own file in their own iCloud, nothing passes through longbook's server, and the statements
in the documents folder are readable. The hosted doors are for when the folder is out of
reach — a phone, a browser, a scheduler in the cloud. The guide, the schema and the tag
library in the folder are kept current by the app, which rewrites them whenever it opens:
read them there, and never edit them.

A statement pasted or attached into the chat is already in front of you — the client
extracted it. `read_document` is for files in the vault's documents folder; do not call it
for a file that is not there.

## The first run — when the folder is empty

An empty `commitments` array and one sentence like "Read my 6-month bank statement and help
me set up my longbook" — the prompt `Set up my longbook` — means you are setting someone up. The app is holding a waiting
screen until this folder holds real commitments. Until then they are looking at a door, so do
the whole job in one sitting rather than handing back a half-filled file. The order below is
the order; each step is the ground the next stands on.

**0. Read `to_fill_in` first.** Setup may have asked the owner what they pay for, and the
names they ticked — "Home rent", "Cook salary", "Wife health insurance" — wait there without
an amount or a day. Both doors show the same list three ways: appended to the server's
instructions at connect, in `whoami`, and in every `commitments` answer beside its
`to_fill_in_note` (the Mac door reads the list into its instructions when the server
starts; `whoami` is always current). Those names come first, before anything else the
statements hold:

- **Search every statement for each one by name, loosely.** "Cook salary" is a UPI to a
  person on the 1st of every month; "Wife health insurance" is one premium line to an
  insurer in one month. When you find one, write it with `add_commitments` under that same
  name — paid rows at their real dates, then promote what repeats — and the app drops it
  from the list. Never write a stranger beside a name that is waiting.
- **Ask for the rest in one table**, one row per name still open, and say a spoken answer
  is fine — most clients take voice, and a rough answer beats none:

  | commitment | your question | your best guess |
  |---|---|---|
  | Wife health insurance | Which insurer, how much, and which month? | HDFC Ergo, about ₹18,000, March — the one line on 15/03 fits |

- **If the statements do not reach far enough** — a yearly premium outside the window, a
  name with no line at all — ask for older or longer statements before you guess. A guess
  written as a fact is the one mistake the owner cannot see in the Proposals screen.

**Setup's hints come with them.** Setup also asked which accounts the owner pays from and who
they pay, and kept the answers in `hints` — accounts by their kind, "Savings account",
"Credit card", and people by their role, "Maid", "Cook". Hints are not accounts or people:
nothing is billed to one. Read each statement with them in mind — a monthly payment to Sunita
may be the cook, the statement's account may be the savings account — and add the account or
person under the name the statement or the owner gives (`add_account`, `add_person`,
"HDFC savings 4521", "Sunita"), never under the hint's own word. Both doors show them beside
`to_fill_in`: in the instructions at connect, in `whoami`, and in every `commitments`
answer with its `hints_note`. An older setup wrote accounts and people by kind and role as
real rows instead: put each statement on the account of its kind and rename that account to
the statement's own first (`update_account`); then write its charges under the new name, since
a charge written to a name the memory does not hold makes a new account. Rename a role's person
with `update_person` once the owner gives the name. "Self" is the owner. Never add either
twice, and never add the owner again.

**1. Say where you are in time.** Before reading a line, name what the statement covers and
where today is: "HDFC savings, 1–31 July 2026; today is 4 September, so this is two months
back." Everything you write from it is dated inside that window, and a report about it is
about July, not about now.

**2. Write every charge as a fact.** A statement is evidence of the past: every line on it
proves a charge happened, on a date, for an amount, from an account. Write each one that is
a charge as a one-time commitment at its real date and amount, `paid: true`, `basis:
"statement"`, on the statement's account, with your best-guess category — and do not ask
permission for a charge that already cleared. Guess by what a wrong guess would cost: copy the
amount, the date, the account and the currency as printed, and never guess them; guess the
name, the category and which commitment a line belongs to, write them, and show them in the
table. A person a line names is a member, as printed; a role for them is a question, their
place is not. Money in — salary, a refund, interest — is
written too, as a one-time row with `direction: "in"`; it never counts as spending. Every
other line is a row, an ATM withdrawal and a card bill payment included; a line is a
`direction: "transfer"` only by the Transfers rule. The method and the worked lines are in `Importing statements` below.

**3. Set what comes round.** A payee the statements show at least three times, a steady
month, quarter or year apart, repeats: `promote_to_recurring` it now. So does one the bank's
own marker names (AUTOPAY, MANDATE, SI, NACH, EMI) or one that repeats by nature — a premium,
an EMI, rent, a salary to a person — even seen once or twice: promoted as a guess, its
`name` ending " (Guessed)" and its `notes` opening "Guessed: " and the reason, per
`Importing statements`. A promotion keeps every charge exactly as it was and plans ahead as
far as the owner says, 24 months if they do not. A repeat that stopped is promoted too, with
`ends_on` at its last charge. List each one in the table, so the owner can undo it. Where
writes are proposals — a sign-in or a key — the rows are not in the memory until the owner's
app applies them, so there are no ids to promote yet: list these repeats as ones you will
set, and promote them after the owner answers, once `commitments` shows the rows.

**4. Ask about Members, and say what they are.** Most owners have never met the idea, so
say it in a sentence: longbook can remember who a payment is for — a Member is a person in
their life, a spouse, a child, a parent, someone they employ — and once a charge is tied to
one, longbook answers "how much do I spend on her?" in one place: health insurance for a
wife, school fees for a son, a helper's salary. Then ask whether they would like to add
anyone; first names are enough. Name a member only when they do.

**5. Show the table.** Call `tags` — it carries every category with its icon — and lay out
every category you chose with how many charges and the total in each, the names and
categories you guessed, and the repeats you set; list every charge you could not place, with
its date and amount, at the bottom. Ask which are wrong, what the unplaced ones were, and how
often each charge seen once or twice comes round, with your guess. Say it can be answered out
loud: most clients take voice, and a rough answer beats a considered one. Every import, not
only the first.

**6. Correct and complete.** Apply what they said — categories, members, and each
commitment's notes: its three details that matter, as far as the source or the owner states
them (see `Notes` below) — in one batched `update_commitment` pass. Undo a repeat the
owner says is not one. Invent nothing they did not say.

**7. Promote the rest on a yes.** For each further repeat the owner confirms,
`promote_to_recurring` it, planned as far as they say, 24 months if they do not. Say how
far you planned.

**Then the reports draw themselves.** longbook writes one per calendar month the rows now
cover as fact — twelve months of statements is twelve reports — the next time the owner
opens it. You write none; `reports` reads them back. The modules each holds, and what to
do with them, are in `Reading reports` below.

**Then say you are done**, and name what they can look at: how many commitments, how many
months the reports will cover, how far the plans reach, and the two or three things you
noticed that they may want to change.

## The working method

1. **Read first.** `commitments` (status "all") and `search` before any write — or the
   file itself. Match by name, loosely: "Netflix", "NETFLIX.COM" and "Netflix India" are one
   commitment. Members and accounts match by `name_key` (trimmed, lowercased name).
   **Name a commitment as the owner would say it** — "Netflix", "Car EMI", "Term insurance" —
   never as the statement prints it; a detail worth keeping goes in its notes.
2. **Update over add.** When a row exists, `update_commitment` it; never create a twin.
   A new card is an update to `account`; a new price is an update to `amount`, which
   reaches only the planned charges from today on — the past is never repriced. An
   account's own name, type, notes (its card name and any other detail, one per line),
   balance with its day, the person it belongs to and its linked account change with
   `update_account`; a person's name, email and tag with `update_person`. `accounts`
   and `people` read them back. A statement's closing balance is its account's
   `balance`, dated the statement's last day: set it with `update_account` after the
   statement's charges are written — the app's own importer does the same — and skip it
   only when the statement prints none.
3. **Every charge is a row.** History is exactly the rows before today; the plan is exactly
   the rows from today on; nothing is computed from a rule. A charge you cannot prove repeats
   is a `once` row at its real date and amount. Doubt is not a reason to skip; it is a
   reason to write `once`.
4. **Write in one batch, then stop.** `add_commitments` takes up to 200 rows in one call;
   a whole year of statements is one or two calls. Then say: "Review the change in the app's
   Proposals screen — keep it or undo it there." Do not re-read and rewrite to "check your
   work"; the owner reviews, not you.
5. **Facts first, then what comes round, then the question.** Write what the statement
   proves; `promote_to_recurring` a payee it shows at least three times, a steady month,
   quarter or year apart, and one the bank marks or that repeats by nature, as a guess named
   so when fewer than three sightings back it; show each, and ask about the rest. Where writes are
   proposals, promote once `commitments` shows the rows the app applied. A promotion keeps
   every fact. What comes back unanswered stays `once`, and goes in the summary for the
   owner to promote later, in the app or through you.
6. **Never invent a fact.** No amounts the source did not show, no dates it did not carry, no
   members or accounts the owner did not name. A guess at a name, a category or a clear
   repeat is fine when you show it; a guess at a fact is not.
7. **Nothing is written unasked, and nothing runs out silently.** The app keeps no plan
   ahead on its own: what is planned is what someone wrote. Plan as far as the owner asks
   (24 months when they do not say), say how far you planned, and when `commitments` or
   `upcoming` names a plan running short, offer to extend it with `set_planned_count`,
   or `add_charges` for named days.

## Prompts — what the owner asks, and the procedure for each

The owner gives their AI one of these, word for word or in their own words. Each has a
procedure, step by step: `read_guide` with the prompt's name or the owner's words returns
it with the chapter it builds on, Claude lists the prompts in its menu, and `prompts.json`,
beside this file, holds them all. Follow the procedure with every rule in this guide. In the
procedures, "the Mac connection" is the first door, the server inside the longbook app; "a
sign-in" is the second, and "a key" the third. The owner sees each prompt's result in the
Automations section of the app and the website, and copies the prompt from there.

**Setting up**

- **Set up my longbook** — "Read my 6-month bank statement and help me set up my longbook", or
  "Read my 12-month bank statement and help me set up my longbook", or "Set up my longbook".
  Your longbook filled from your statements: every charge on record, the names you picked in
  setup filled in where your statements or your answers show them, each account's closing
  balance set, the charges that clearly repeat planned ahead, and the rest set to repeat once
  you confirm them. It waits in the Proposals screen for you to keep. Builds on "first-run".
- **Add my statement** — "Add my statement in my longbook", or "Update my longbook from my
  statements", or "Add my statement". Every charge on the statement recorded as paid, money in
  kept apart, the account's balance updated, the charges that clearly repeat set to continue,
  and the rest once you confirm them. Builds on "importing-statements".
- **Categorise my longbook** — "Categorise my longbook". Every commitment without a category
  gets one. Your AI shows you the ones it guessed, so you can correct any. Builds on
  "categorise-my-longbook".
- **Add a month report in my longbook** — "Add September month report in my longbook". The
  month's statements recorded, the charges they prove confirmed, and each account's balance
  set. longbook draws that month's report, with "Not yet confirmed" beside the total until
  every charge in it is confirmed. Builds on "month-report".

**Keeping it current**

- **Add email invoices in my longbook** — "Add email invoices in my longbook". This month's
  bank alerts, receipts, bills and money in from your mail, each recorded once, with nothing
  doubled. Needs the owner's mail, connected to their AI. Builds on "daily-email-round".
- **Set up a daily longbook email round** — "Go to longbook.app/mcp and set up a daily email
  round for my longbook, as longbook recommends". Your AI reads your mail every morning at 6
  and records the money that moved, so your longbook stays current without you asking. Needs
  the owner's mail, connected to their AI, and scheduled tasks in their AI's app. Builds on
  "daily-email-round".
- **Add document invoices in my longbook** — "Add document invoices in my longbook". The
  invoices, receipts and bills you attach, or keep in the longbook documents folder, recorded
  as charges with the file's name in their notes, without doubling what your statements or mail
  already recorded. Builds on "document-invoices".
- **Add a commitment or an expense** — "Add a commitment in my longbook", or "Add an expense in
  my longbook", or "Add my new gym membership to my longbook". A new commitment planned ahead,
  or a one-time expense recorded, on the account and for the person you name. Builds on
  "working-method".

**Reading it**

- **What do I pay next?** — "What's my next commitment in my longbook", or "What do I pay
  next?". The next day you owe something, and what is due that day. Nothing in your longbook
  changes.
- **What is coming in the next 30 days?** — "What is coming in my longbook in the next 30
  days?", or "What is coming in the next 30 days?", or "What do I owe this month?". Everything
  due in the next 30 days, or the period you name, by day, with the total per currency. Nothing
  in your longbook changes.
- **What did I spend in a month?** — "What did I spend in July in my longbook?", or "What did I
  spend in July?". What you spent in that month, and what is not yet confirmed. Through the Mac
  connection this comes from longbook's report; otherwise from your charges, including ones
  nobody has confirmed yet. Nothing in your longbook changes. Builds on "reading-reports".
- **What renews this year?** — "What renews this year in my longbook?", or "What renews this
  year?", or "Which premiums are due before March?". Your yearly, half-yearly and quarterly
  payments due in the next 12 months, or before the day you name, in date order. Nothing in
  your longbook changes.
- **Make my weekly longbook page** — "Make my weekly longbook page", or "Give me my longbook
  week". One page for the week: what is due in the next 7 days, what you spent last week, what
  renews in the next 30 days, and anything waiting for you. Nothing in your longbook changes.

**Reports**

- **Create a report in my longbook** — "Create a report in my longbook". A report over the
  days, accounts, people and categories you choose, on the Reports screen the next time the app
  is open. It counts confirmed charges only. Builds on "create-a-report".
- **Make a report of my trip** — "Make a report of my Goa trip in my longbook", or "Make a
  report of my Goa trip". A report of your trip's spending on the Reports screen, filling in as
  the trip's charges are confirmed. Builds on "create-a-report".

**Housekeeping**

- **Tidy my longbook** — "Tidy my longbook". Doubled charges, bank-style names and odd
  categories found, and fixed once you approve each change. Builds on "working-method".
- **Reorganise my longbook** — "Reorganise my longbook". Your whole longbook, once over: names
  as you would say them, every row categorised, people and accounts linked, doubles merged,
  nothing lost. The whole pass waits in Proposals. Builds on "reorganise-my-longbook".
- **Set up a morning brief** — "Set up a morning brief for my longbook", or "Set yourself up
  for a longbook morning brief". A short summary every morning of what is due today and in the
  next 30 days. Nothing in your longbook changes. Needs scheduled tasks in their AI's app.
  Builds on "unattended-runs".

**From your email**

- **Find subscriptions from my email** — "Find subscriptions from my email and add them in my
  longbook". Your subscriptions found in the last 12 months of your mail: each one with its
  receipts as charges, the ones that clearly repeat planned ahead, and trials and price changes
  as the mails state them. Needs the owner's mail, connected to their AI. Builds on
  "daily-email-round".
- **Find expenses from my email** — "Find expenses from my email and add them in my longbook".
  This month's spending from your mail's bank alerts and receipts, each recorded once as a paid
  charge. Needs the owner's mail, connected to their AI. Builds on "daily-email-round".
- **Find invoices from my email** — "Find invoices from my email and add them in my longbook".
  The invoices and receipts in the last 12 months of your mail, each recorded once as a charge,
  paid or due. Needs the owner's mail, connected to their AI. Builds on "daily-email-round".
- **Find insurances from my email** — "Find insurances from my email and add them in my
  longbook". Your insurance policies found in your mail: each with its premiums as charges, its
  next premium planned, and its policy details in its notes. Needs the owner's mail, connected
  to their AI. Builds on "daily-email-round".
- **Find purchases from my email** — "Find purchases from my email and add them in my
  longbook". Your orders from the last 3 months of your mail, each recorded once as a paid
  charge named for what you bought. Needs the owner's mail, connected to their AI. Builds on
  "daily-email-round".
- **Find bills from my email** — "Find bills from my email and add them in my longbook". Your
  bills from the last 3 months of your mail: what you paid recorded, what is due planned, and
  each card's monthly bill kept apart from spending. Needs the owner's mail, connected to their
  AI. Builds on "daily-email-round".
- **Find loans and EMIs from my email** — "Find loans and EMIs from my email and add them in my
  longbook". Your loans and EMIs found in your mail: each loan with its EMIs as charges,
  planned ahead to its end when the mails state it. Needs the owner's mail, connected to their
  AI. Builds on "daily-email-round".
- **Find travel bookings from my email** — "Find travel bookings from my email and add them in
  my longbook". Your bookings from the last 12 months of your mail: flights, trains, hotels and
  cabs, each recorded as a paid charge with where and when. Needs the owner's mail, connected
  to their AI. Builds on "daily-email-round".
- **Find money in from my email** — "Find money in from my email and add them in my longbook".
  Your salary, refunds, interest and other money in from the last 12 months of your mail, kept
  apart from spending. Needs the owner's mail, connected to their AI. Builds on
  "daily-email-round".

## Importing statements — the method, with examples

The owner drops bank and card statements into the vault's `documents/` folder (PDF with
text, `.xlsx`, or `.csv` — nothing else is read; a scanned PDF is refused with the reason)
and says something like "Update my longbook from my statements" or "Add September month
report in my longbook". That is the Mac door; through the hosted doors the statement
arrives attached in the chat, already in front of you.

**A statement is evidence of the past.** Every line on it proves a charge happened, on a
date, for an amount. Record what it proves; do not ask permission for it. "Shall I add
this?" about a charge that already cleared has one answer, and a year of statements asked
that way is an interrogation, not an import.

**Ask what the paper cannot say.** A statement carries a payee string, not what the charge
was, who it was for, or whether it repeats — and those are the questions worth a person's
attention. Collect them while you classify, ask them in one batch when you have finished
reading, short enough to answer out loud, and write once. A good one names the evidence and
asks the unknown: "₹5,400 to a name I cannot place, twice since March — what is it, and is
it for anyone in particular?"

**Whether it repeats is settled by three kinds of evidence, in order.** The bank's own
marker in the narration; the same name at about the same amount three or more times at a
steady rhythm; a payee that repeats by nature, seen once or twice. Write the lines first,
each as a one-time row; `promote_to_recurring` each commitment the evidence makes and show
it in the table — one backed by fewer than three sightings as a guess, its `name` ending
" (Guessed)" and its `notes` opening "Guessed: " and the reason, so the owner sees it for
what it is and renames it to keep it. Where writes are proposals, the rows reach the memory
only when the owner's app applies them: list the repeats, and promote them once
`commitments` shows the rows. A promotion keeps every charge the statement proved, exactly
as written, and plans ahead from the last of them. With nobody in the conversation to
answer, do not wait: leave the rows `once` and propose the promotions in your note, per
`Unattended runs`.

This is the whole flow:

1. `list_documents` → `read_document` each (long files page through `next_offset`; keep
   asking until it is null). Credit-card statements hold the card's real charges; the bank
   statement's "card bill payment" line is a line like any other, not a transfer. It is
   written as the statement prints it, and a charge of the card is written from the card's
   own statement: if both statements are imported, say so in your report, because the
   same money then shows on the bank and on the card.
2. `commitments` with status "all", so what is already there is known — a line that
   belongs to a commitment that exists is `add_charges` on it, paid, basis "statement",
   not a twin.
3. Read every line by the rules below. They are the same words longbook's own reader
   follows, so a statement read by you and one read by the app agree. Every line is a
   one-time row at its real date and amount, `paid: true`, `basis: "statement"`; its kind
   decides what you say about it and what you promote afterwards.

   **Reading the lines.**

   - Every dated line with an amount is one charge: never totalled, never skipped for being
     small, however many there are.
   - A reversal or a refund is its own line, as printed, never netted against the charge it
     undoes.
   - The running balance is never a charge; the closing balance and the day it was true are
     kept, as printed, and never worked out.
   - The statement's own columns settle which way the money went before its words do: a line in
     the credit column, or after which the balance rose, is money in whatever the narration
     says; a line in the debit column is money out even when the narration reads like a
     receipt.
   - Never invent a line, a date or an amount, and never total or convert anything.

   **The kinds.**

   - Every line is one kind. spend: money that bought something, or money moved out. fee: a
     bank charge, tax or interest paid. for_member: money paid for or to a person in the
     owner's life, naming the person. income: salary, a refund, cashback, interest received,
     anything credited. Whether a line is a transfer is never a kind: the Transfers rule
     decides it.

   **Transfers.**

   - A charge is a transfer only when both its account and the other side's account belong to a
     person whose relationship is Self. Nothing else is a transfer: not an ATM withdrawal, a
     wallet load, a payment through CRED or of a card bill, and not words in the line.
   - longbook applies this by itself. Setting a person to Self, or an account's owner, makes
     the matching charges transfers; clearing it returns them to money out or money in as the
     statement printed them. Write direction "transfer" only for a line that meets the rule;
     any other line is out (no direction) or "in".

   **People.**

   - A person's name is written exactly as the line prints it, title-cased, even when the bank
     cut it short: "HOORNAPRIYA AMBA FUE" stays "Hoornapriya Amba Fue". It is never completed,
     never shortened further, and never guessed from an amount or a role.
   - The account holder is the person the statement belongs to, named in its header: written
     exactly as printed, in holder, and null when the header prints none. The holder is a
     person in the longbook with the relationship Self, and the statement's own account is
     theirs. A line's person who shares at least two words with the holder, in any order, is
     the holder, never a second person; a bank account printed beside that person is the
     holder's account.
   - Every person a line names is a member, once, however often seen, whether the money went
     out or came in.
   - A merchant, a shop or a company is never a person; a line that names no person names no
     member.

   **The other side.**

   - The other side of a line is named only when the line prints it; otherwise there is none,
     never a guess.
   - A bank's IFSC code printed on the line names that bank: UTIB is Axis Bank, BARB Bank of
     Baroda, HDFC HDFC Bank, ICIC ICICI Bank, SBIN State Bank of India, KKBK Kotak, SURY
     Suryoday Small Finance Bank, and so on. An account is written as its bank, its kind when
     printed, and the last four digits after "••" ("Axis savings ••1234", "HDFC card ••4417",
     "Paytm wallet"); never a UPI id, a phone number or a full number.
   - When a line prints both a person and that person's bank account, the person is the other
     side and the account is kept beside them as the person's bank account.
   - The owner's own other account, on a payment to their own savings, card or wallet or on a
     card bill payment, is the other side too, named the same way; it is never left out for
     being the owner's or for being seen once.
   - A merchant or a shop is never the other side, and neither is the statement's own account.

   **Names.**

   - A charge's name is what the owner would call it, two to four words: "Netflix", "House
     rent", "Axis card bill".
   - A name never carries an amount, a currency sign, a cycle, a card or app name in brackets,
     or anything in brackets at all.
   - A person's charge is named by the person, as printed.
   - When a charge's name is the person's name, it is "Payment to X" for money out and "Payment
     from X" for money in, X being the person. Every repeat naming that person takes the same
     name.

   **What comes round.**

   - The bank's own marker in the narration (AUTOPAY, MANDATE, SI, NACH, ACH, ECS, STANDING
     INSTRUCTION, EMI) makes a commitment, even when seen once.
   - The same name at about the same amount, three or more times at a steady rhythm (monthly
     about 30 days apart, yearly about 365, quarterly 91, half-yearly 183) makes a commitment.
   - A payee that repeats by nature, seen once or twice, makes a commitment: insurance or a
     premium, an EMI or a loan, rent, school or fees, society maintenance, a domain or hosting,
     telecom, a utility, a salary to a person.
   - A commitment backed by fewer than three sightings is guessed, with a reason in one
     sentence naming the evidence and the cycle assumed ("Seen once with the bank's mandate
     mark; yearly assumed from the insurer's name"); three or more at a steady rhythm is not a
     guess.
   - The cycle comes from the interval when seen more than once, and from the words otherwise:
     an EMI, rent, a salary, telecom, a utility and maintenance are monthly; insurance and a
     domain are yearly unless the amount reads monthly.
   - A repeat that has stopped ends at its last charge.
   - Everything else stays a one-time charge; nothing becomes a repeat from its amount alone.

   **Notes.**

   - Every charge's note is "Statement line: " followed by the line as printed, with reference,
     account and card numbers removed.
   - A guessed commitment's name ends with " (Guessed)" and its notes begin with the line
     "Guessed: " and the reason; the owner's edit of the name removes both.
   - A commitment's notes hold only what the statement states, as the three details that
     matter: never a guess, never a "Paid by" line, never a reference beyond the statement.

   **Accounts.**

   - The statement's own account is an account in the longbook, named from its header (bank,
     kind, last four digits), owned by the holder, with its closing balance and the day it was
     true.
   - An account's name never carries a person's name: "HDFC Bank", with the person as its
     owner. Two accounts at one bank that print no digits are told apart by their owner, not by
     their name.
   - Every account printed on another side of a line, the other side itself or a person's bank
     account, is an account in the longbook too, owned by the person when the line names one.

   What each kind becomes: spend, fee and for_member are one-time rows, a for_member row
   with `member` the person as printed; income is the same row with `direction: "in"`, kept
   beside spending and never added to it. No line is skipped for being the owner's own
   money moving: an ATM withdrawal, a wallet load and a card bill payment are one-time rows
   like the rest. A line is written with `direction: "transfer"` only by the Transfers
   rule: both its account and the other side's account owned by a person tagged self. Then
   it is shown on the timeline, never in spending, never in money in. longbook applies the
   rule itself once the people and the owners are set. If the owner
   said "only the commitments" or "skip food delivery", honour that; otherwise every line
   is a fact, however small.
4. Model honestly, the way the ledger works (see "The past is stored"): every line paid,
   with `basis: "statement"`, at the date and amount on the paper; `ends_on` when the
   source shows an end; a plan only as far as the owner asked. Each row wears the name the
   Names rules give it — "Netflix", not "UPI/4521/NETFLIX.COM" — and its charge's `note`
   is the statement line, per the Notes rules, with every reference, account and card
   number removed.
5. Tags from the library first (the icon then resolves in the app on its own); invent only
   when nothing fits. A commitment's `notes` hold its three details that matter, one per
   line, only as far as the statement states them — `Notes` below lists them by category;
   a guessed commitment's notes open with the "Guessed: " line first.
6. People and accounts, by the People and Accounts rules: `add_person` every person a line
   names, as printed, once; `add_account` the statement's own account, and every account
   printed on another side of a line — the other side itself, or the bank account printed
   beside a person — with `member` the person when the line names one. The statement's
   closing balance and date go on its account as `balance` and `balance_date`.
7. Write, show, promote, ask, correct. One `add_commitments` call (or a few, back to
   back) with every line; then, when the statement prints a closing balance, one
   `update_account` on the statement's account — `balance` the closing figure,
   `balance_date` the statement's last day — so the account reads as the statement left
   it; `promote_to_recurring` for each commitment the three kinds of evidence make, the
   guessed ones named so; the table of what you chose and guessed; one message carrying
   every question the reading left open — what an unidentifiable charge was, who a person
   is to the owner — and the corrections in one pass. Then stop and report: how many rows,
   what was promoted, which of those were guesses and how far each is planned, what you
   skipped and why, and the balance you set with its day — or that the statement printed
   none.
8. Finish the picture if asked: two or three `leave_insight` notes. The reports for the
   months the statements cover are longbook's to draw, and it draws them.

### Worked lines

A bank statement, twelve months, the lines that matter and what each becomes:

```
01/07/2026  NETFLIX.COM                649.00  (and 01/06, 01/05 … 01/08/2025)
→ twelve one-time rows, one per charge, paid, basis statement, tag streaming. Seen twelve
  times a month apart and still going: promote_to_recurring the twelve as "Netflix",
  monthly, and show it — the twelve stay as they are, the plan continues from 01/08/2026
  for 24 months.

05/07/2026  HDFC BANK EMI 884211       12,340.00  (every 5th since 05/02/2025)
→ eighteen one-time rows, then promoted monthly, tag emi, notes "Lender: HDFC Bank" and
  "Loan account: 4211", one per line. ends_on only if the tenure is known. Never the whole
  loan account number: the last four digits are the most that leaves the statement.

15/03/2026  HDFC ERGO HEALTH PREMIUM   18,450.00  (once in twelve months)
→ one row, paid, tag insurance. A premium repeats by nature: promoted yearly as a guess,
  name "HDFC Ergo health (Guessed)", notes "Guessed: Seen once; yearly assumed from the
  insurer's name" — the next charge planned for 15/03/2027. Its other notes — "Policy
  number: …", "Policy name: …", "Document: documents/hdfc-ergo-health.pdf" — only as far
  as a policy document in documents/, or the owner, states them.

12/01/2026  STAR HEALTH PREMIUM        9,200.00  and 12/07/2026 STAR HEALTH PREMIUM 9,200.00
→ two rows, paid, tag insurance. Seen twice: promoted custom, custom_cycle_days 183, as a
  guess — "Star Health (Guessed)", notes "Guessed: Seen twice, half a year apart; the same
  rhythm assumed".

01/07/2026  UPI-RAMESH K-cook           6,000.00  (every 1st)
→ add_person "Ramesh K", as printed, never "Ramesh" or "the cook"; rows with member
  "Ramesh K", then promoted monthly, tag salary, notes "Role: cook". Who he is to the
  owner is the question, not whether he is in People.

03/06/2026  GODADDY.COM                3,597.00  (once; the owner says it was a 3-year deal)
→ one row, promoted custom, custom_cycle_days 1095, tag domain & hosting, notes
  "Registrar: GoDaddy". The owner said so, so it is no guess. A 24-month plan writes
  nothing more: the next renewal is three years out, and add_charges writes it the day the
  owner asks.

10/06/2026  IRCTC                      4,560.00
→ one row, tag travel. It stays once.

SPOTIFY 119.00 on the 12th, Sept 2025 through April 2026, then nothing
→ eight rows, then promoted monthly with ends_on 2026-04-12: one commitment, eight charges
  on record, nothing planned past the day it stopped.

02/07/2026  APPLE.COM/BILL             0.00   then 02/08/2026 APPLE.COM/BILL 99.00
→ two rows — the first is a charge of zero, which is what a trial is — tag subscription or
  storage; say which you chose. Seen twice, a month apart: promoted monthly as a guess,
  "Apple (Guessed)", notes "Guessed: Seen twice, a month apart; the same rhythm assumed".

28/06/2026  CREDIT CARD PAYMENT        42,310.00   → one row, a charge like any other (not a transfer:
                                                     the card is no Self account)
30/06/2026  SALARY CREDIT             1,50,000.00  → one row, direction "in" (money in, kept apart)
14/06/2026  ATM WDL                   10,000.00    → one row, a charge
```

The questions to the owner after the facts are written, in shape — one message, nothing
about a charge the statement already settles:

> The year is in. Three things and I can finish. (1) ₹5,400 to a name I cannot place, twice
> since March — what is it, and who is it for? (2) Hoornapriya Amba Fue is paid ₹2,000 on the
> 7th of every month, so she is in People as printed and the payment is set to continue —
> who is she to you? (3) Netflix, rent, the cook, Airtel and the society dues come round
> every month, so they are set to continue; say if any is not. HDFC Ergo and Star Health are
> set as guesses, yearly and half-yearly, with the reason in their notes: rename either to
> keep it, or say if it is not one. Say it out loud if that is easier; rough answers are fine.

The summary to the owner once the answers are in, in shape:

> 87 charges from the statement, all recorded as paid. Thirteen of them turned out to be
> nine commitments that repeat — Netflix, rent, the cook, Airtel, the society dues, Adobe,
> Amazon Prime, Claude, and the two premiums, those two as guesses named so — each planned
> 24 months ahead; Spotify
> stopped in April and is on record that way. Twelve salary credits are in as money in,
> kept apart from spending. Two card bill payments and three ATM withdrawals are in as
> ordinary rows, none of them a transfer. HDFC savings now stands at ₹1,23,456 as of
> 30 June, the statement's closing balance. Review it in the Proposals screen — keep or undo
> it there.

### Statements that arrive as Excel or CSV

Columns are usually Date, Narration/Description, Debit, Credit, Balance. Debit lines are
charges; Credit lines are money in, written with `direction: "in"`, unless they are the
owner's own transfer. Dates come in the bank's format (DD/MM/YYYY is common in India; read the
header row and one known date before assuming). A narration often carries the payee in the
middle of a reference string — "UPI/123456789/NETFLIX/…" — so match on the word, not the
line.

## The past is stored, the future is written — nothing is computed

Every charge is a row in `charges[]`, keyed by (commitment_id, date). longbook computes no
occurrence from any rule: history is exactly the rows before today, the plan is exactly the
rows from today on, and a commitment with no rows has no charges anywhere — not on the
dashboard, not in a total, not in a report.

- A **commitment** holds only what every charge of it shares: name, `amount` (the price
  now — what a newly planned charge is written at), currency, `billing_cycle`, category,
  member, account, notes, details, status, and `ends_on`. Nothing about an occurrence
  lives there. "Renewing since" is its earliest row. "Next due" is its first unpaid row on
  or after today. "Planned till" is its last row.
- A **charge** holds what is particular: `date`, `amount`, `paid`, `paid_on`, `basis`
  (what backs it), a `note`. **A charge behind today is paid** whatever its row says: the
  money was due and the day has passed, so every reader — the app, every tool here — reads
  it as paid and never calls it an estimate. A row from today on is the plan, and its
  `paid` mark is what counts.
- **A commitment is what still lies ahead.** A recurring one is a commitment while it is
  active. A one-time one is a commitment until its charge is behind today or marked paid;
  after that it is that one charge and nothing more — `commitments` leaves it out and
  counts it, `charges` reads it. A statement of five hundred lines is five hundred charges,
  not five hundred commitments.
- **Nothing is written unasked.** A recurring commitment is planned when it is created —
  `plan_months` charges from `first_charge`, or exactly `plan_count` of them, 24 months
  when nobody says. A plan grows only when someone asks: `set_planned_count` sets how many
  charges stand from today on (240 at most) — more are written a cycle apart after the
  last, unpaid planned rows past the count are unwritten, paid and hand-set rows stay;
  `add_charges` writes named days. The app never extends a plan on its own; when one runs
  short it says so, and `commitments` and `upcoming` name it. A one-time commitment is
  one charge on its `date`.
- **Changing a commitment changes what is shared.** Its `amount` reaches only charges that
  are unpaid, planned and dated from today (or `from`) on. Nothing before today ever
  changes because a commitment was edited, and a charge someone priced by hand, or a
  statement proved, keeps its number.
- **Changing a charge changes that charge.** `update_charge` changes one charge where it
  sits — its amount, its day, its paid mark, the day the money moved, its note; with
  `and_later` the unpaid planned rows after it follow, a cycle apart, and keep their
  amounts. A day that already holds a charge is refused. `mark_paid` remains the
  one-field way to mark.
- **`status` pauses, resumes or cancels:** pausing or cancelling unwrites the unpaid
  planned charges after today and keeps what happened; back to active plans nothing —
  `set_planned_count` continues it. A cancelled commitment's past charges still count,
  because they did. `ends_on` is a known end: nothing is planned past it, a charge on the
  day itself still lands. `free_trial` is a mark on the row — true while the owner calls it
  a free trial, shown as a pill — and never a charge row.
- Cycles: `monthly` and `yearly` step by calendar months, the day clamped into a short
  month (the 31st becomes the 28th); `custom` steps by `custom_cycle_days`; `once` never
  steps. The rhythm only matters when a plan is written.
- Amounts are per currency, never converted. A USD subscription and an INR rent are two
  totals, always. A charge may state its own currency when it differs from its commitment's.

## Tags — what kind of thing each row is

Every commitment, member and account can wear one tag, and `tags[]` is the vault's own
vocabulary for them: a name and an icon. A tag says what kind of thing a row is; it never
gives a row a shape. **No tag carries a template**: what is particular about a commitment —
a policy number, a lender, a plan — is the lines of its notes, three at most (see `Notes`
below); what is particular about an account — a card's printed name, a billing day — is the
lines of its notes too; and a member carries a name, a tag, an email and linked accounts,
nothing else. A template a vault still holds on any tag is read as none.

Tag names match loosely — "Insurance", "insurance" and " insurance " are one tag — so a
library name written in any case still picks up its icon. An icon is an SF Symbol name from the
library list above — a new tag takes one of those, or none. Prefer the library; invent only
when nothing fits ("colony kitty", "pet care"). A vault that grows "Home", "Comms",
"Househelps", "Social Media" and "AI subscription" as its own tags is a real vault, and
longbook keeps those; but "telecom", "salary", "social media" and "ai" were already there
with icons, and an AI that knows the library saves the owner the tidy-up.

`rename_tag` renames a tag in the vault's own vocabulary and carries every row wearing it,
the owner's tag groups too; `delete_tag` removes it and the rows it wore are left with no
category. Both only on the owner's word — a tag the owner typed is theirs.

The library, with icons (SF Symbol names):

commitment tags:
- food & groceries [fork.knife]
- shopping [bag]
- subscription [arrow.triangle.2.circlepath]
- streaming [play.tv]
- software [app.badge]
- ai [sparkles]
- social media [at]
- telecom [antenna.radiowaves.left.and.right]
- insurance [shield.checkered]
- emi [building.columns]
- rent [house]
- utility [bolt]
- salary [banknote]
- education [graduationcap]
- fees [doc.text]
- membership [checkmark.seal]
- domain & hosting [globe]
- travel [airplane]
- health & fitness [heart]
- home [wrench.and.screwdriver]
- vehicle [car]
- gift [gift]
- donation [heart.circle]
- warranty & amc [checkmark.shield]
- tax [percent]

member tags:
- self [person.crop.circle]
- family [person.2]
- household help [person.badge.clock]
- team [briefcase]
- vendor [shippingbox]
- professional [person.text.rectangle]
- landlord [building.2]
- tenant [key]
- friend [hand.wave]

account tags:
- credit card [creditcard.fill]
- debit card [creditcard]
- bank account [building.columns]
- upi [qrcode]
- wallet [wallet.pass]
- cash [banknote]
- brokerage [chart.line.uptrend.xyaxis]
- loan account [doc.plaintext]

A tag for a real household, from a real vault's shape: insurance is usually the biggest
cluster (term life, health floater, car, two-wheeler, home — most yearly, some half-yearly);
home holds rent, society maintenance, electricity, gas, water, internet; telecom holds two
or three phone plans; salary holds the cook, the cleaner, the driver; subscription, streaming,
ai, software and social media hold the digital stack; domain & hosting runs on 1–3 year
cycles; travel and gift are mostly once.

## Categorise my longbook — the rows that wear no category

"Categorise my longbook" is one pass over every commitment that has no tag — the ones the
app lists under "No category". `commitments` with status "all" gives every row, past and
planned, with its tag or none; `charges` over a wide window shows what each one has been
paying, which is often the clue. `tags` gives the vault's own names beside the library's:
those first, a new one only when nothing fits.

Where the name says what the row is, write it: "Netflix" is streaming, "Airtel" is telecom,
"HDFC Ergo" is insurance, "Ramesh" paid on the 1st is salary. For the rest, guess from the
name and what the row has been paying, and write your guess. One batched
`update_commitment` pass, each with its `tag`; then show every guess in one table —
name, date, amount, the category you chose — ask the owner to correct any that are wrong,
and say a spoken answer is fine. Apply the corrections in one more pass, and stop: "review it
in Proposals". A tag the owner names is theirs, in their words.

## Reorganise my longbook — the whole book, once over

"Reorganise my longbook" is one pass over everything, the way the owner would keep it if
they had an afternoon: names as they would say them, every row in a category, people and
accounts linked, doubles merged, nothing lost. longbook's own AI runs it from the app's
Automations screen; the owner's AI runs it from the prompt; both follow this chapter, and
every change waits in Proposals, where the owner keeps or undoes the whole pass at once.

Read everything first: `commitments` with status "all", `charges` over a wide window,
`people`, `accounts`, `tags`. Then, in this order:

1. **Names.** A name written the bank's way — "NETFLIX.COM 4402", "ACH DEBIT HDFC ERGO" —
   becomes the name the owner would say: "Netflix", "HDFC Ergo car insurance". A person's
   name stays their name. Never shorten what is already a name.
2. **Categories.** Every commitment wears a tag: the book's own words first, then the
   library's; a new one only when nothing fits. Two tags that mean one thing — "Streaming"
   and "OTT" — become one, by `rename_tag` onto the one kept, which moves every wearer.
   Doubt is a tag too: guess from the name and what the row has been paying, and say so in
   the reason.
3. **People and accounts.** A commitment paid to or for a person is linked to them,
   `add_person` first when the book has no such person; a commitment the charges show on
   one account is linked to that account. A card the book shows paying a bank is linked to
   it. Never guess a person from a role or an amount: only a name the row itself carries.
4. **Doubles.** One payee under two commitments: give both the same right name and
   category, and say in the reason that they are one — the owner merges them in the app.
   One charge recorded twice, the same day and amount under two commitments, both paid:
   `remove_charges` the copy on the newer commitment. Nothing else is ever removed.
5. **Notes.** A note that holds a card number, a whole account number or a password is
   rewritten without it. Otherwise notes are the owner's words; leave them.

What a reorganisation never changes: an amount, a date, a cycle, a status, an ends_on, a
planned count, a balance, a charge that happened. A row already right is left alone. One
pass, batched; then stop, and say in plain words what was renamed, categorised, linked and
merged, and that it all waits in Proposals.

## People and accounts

`members[]` is who a commitment is **for** — a child's school fee, a parent's health
premium, a team member's software seat. `accounts[]` is what it is **billed to** — a card, a
bank account, UPI, a wallet, cash. Either can be a placeholder (`is_incomplete: true`, just
a name) until the owner fills it in; both `add_commitments` and `update_commitment` make
placeholders for a `member` or `account` name that does not exist yet; `update_account`'s
`member` and `linked_to` need a name the memory holds. `accounts` and `people` list
every one with what it holds.
`add_person` and `add_account` make a person or an account the owner named, with what is
known — a name already held is refused rather than doubled; `update_person` and
`update_account` change one that exists. Name a person only when the owner did.

**A star keeps one first.** The owner stars the people and accounts they look at most:
`starred: true` lists them first on People and Accounts, and only starred ones stand in
the Mac sidebar. `update_person` and `update_account` take `starred` in their set; set it
only when the owner asks, never to tidy.

**Hints are not people or accounts.** `hints[]` holds what setup asked: people by role
("Cook") and accounts by kind ("Savings account"). Use them to read statements, and add the
real person or account under the name a statement or the owner gives; leave the hint alone.

**A person's tag is their role in the owner's finances** — landlord, household help,
family, tenant, a professional they pay. Set it with `update_person` when the owner says
it ("Ramesh is our cook" → household help); never guess it from a payment. The library's
member tags first, a new one only when nothing fits. A member carries a name, a tag, an
email and linked accounts — the accounts that belong to them — and nothing else: what the
owner says about a person's role belongs in the notes of the commitment it is about
("Role: cook" on the salary).

Accounts carry identification only: display name ("Amex 1007"), institution ("American
Express"), `last4`, a nickname, a tag, `notes`, and the person it belongs to. What is
particular about an account is the lines of its notes, one per line as `Label: value`. A
card's **card name** is one — the product printed on it, "Card name: Platinum Reserve",
never a number. It is what to read, with the institution, when the owner asks "any offers
on my cards?". Write it, and any other detail, with `update_account`'s `notes`,
rewritten as the account now stands.

`details` on an account or a member is longbook's own, as on a commitment: `accounts` and
`members` return any a row holds exactly as stored, and no write takes it —
`update_account` and `update_person` refuse a non-empty `card_name` or `details` by name,
and name an empty one, as any key they do not take, under `ignored`.

An account can name its **linked account** — the account it is linked to: a card to the
bank account that pays it, one level deep. The file keeps this under its older key,
`parent_account_id`; `accounts` reads it as `linked_to`, and `update_account` takes
`linked_to`. An account may also carry a `balance` and its
`balance_date` — what it held on that day, as a statement's closing balance or the owner's
own word; write it after importing any statement that prints one, dated the statement's
last day, and never compute anything from it; `accounts` and `whoami` say when the
balance held is older than the newest confirmed charge on that account, and
`add_commitments` and `add_charges` answer with a `balance_note` when the rows just
written outrun it. The owner's own groups ("credit cards", "debit cards",
"household", "team") live in `groups[]` and are labels over existing ids — never create a
record to fill a group.

## The documents folder — the source of past truth

`documents/` beside the memory is where statements, policy PDFs, invoices and receipts
live. It is the permanent record the memory was built from: a statement stays there after it
is imported, so any later question ("what did I pay Star Health in 2025?") can be answered
from the paper, not from memory. When a row comes from a document, cite it: a line of the
commitment's notes names the file by its path (`Document: documents/term-policy.pdf`), and
`_provenance[id].source` says where the write came from (`"documents/hdfc-2026.pdf"`).
Never paste a document's contents into the vault; reference it.

Formats: PDF that carries text, `.xlsx`, `.csv`. A scanned PDF, a `.docx`, a legacy `.xls`
or an image is listed as unsupported with a one-line way out ("save it as .xlsx or CSV") —
the app's own importer reads `.xls`; the documents tool does not. A file still in iCloud and
not yet downloaded is named so and its download nudged — ask again in a moment.

## Document invoices — receipts and bills in the owner's files

"Add document invoices in my longbook" means the files, not the mail: the invoices, receipts
and bills the owner keeps as documents. Where to look, in order: the longbook folder's
`documents/` (`list_documents`, then `read_document` each); the owner's Documents and
Downloads folders only when your own app can read files there — Claude Desktop on a Mac
with file access — because no longbook tool reaches outside `documents/`; through a
hosted door, ask the owner to attach the files to the chat, or to drop them in `documents/`.

An invoice or a receipt is one charge. Paid, at the day it names, when it says paid or that
day has passed; `paid: false` at its due date when the due date is ahead. Name it as the
owner would say it — "Plumber, kitchen tap", never the invoice number — with `basis:
"statement"` (the paper is the evidence), `source: "documents/<file>"` and a
`Document: documents/<file>` line in its notes; the amount, the currency and the day only
as printed. `search` the payee first: a charge already written from a mail or a statement
for that amount and day is the same money, and the invoice gives it the better name and
note — update it, never a twin. When the payee is a commitment the memory holds, the
invoice is that commitment's charge: `add_charges` on it. One batch, then stop: it waits
in Proposals.

## Notes — the three details that matter

A commitment's `notes` holds its three most important details, one per line, each as
`Label: value`. There are no per-category fields; the category decides which three, not the
shape. The owner reads the note whole on the commitment's own page. Examples by category —
pick the three the owner would look for first, and leave out any the source does not state:

- insurance — Policy number; Policy name, the official name as printed; Document, the
  policy's file name in `documents/` ("Document: documents/hdfc-life-policy.pdf")
- emi — Lender; Loan ends; Loan account, last four digits only
- rent — Landlord; Deposit; Lease ends
- food & groceries, shopping — Merchant; Kind; Billed through (a card's or an app's name)
- subscription, streaming, software, ai, social media — Plan; Billed through (App Store,
  Google Play, a card's name); Seats or profiles
- telecom — Provider; Plan; Number, last four digits only
- utility — Provider; Consumer number; Place ("Home", "Office")
- salary — Role; Paid by (UPI, cash, bank transfer); Started
- education, fees — Institution or payee; Student; Term
- membership, health & fitness — Organisation; Membership number; Valid till
- domain & hosting — Registrar; Domain; Auto-renew
- travel — Destination; Dates; Booked through
- home — Kind; Vendor; Invoice, the file name in `documents/`
- vehicle — Vehicle; Registration; Kind (service, insurance, fuel)
- warranty & amc — Item; Vendor; Coverage ends
- tax — Kind; Period; Receipt, the challan's file name in `documents/`
- donation, gift — Organisation or recipient; Occasion or purpose; Receipt, the file name
  in `documents/`
- any other tag — the three the owner would look for first

The rules:

1. **Three lines at most**, one detail to a line — `Policy number: 88213`, never a
   paragraph.
2. **Only what the source states.** When it leaves some out, ask the owner once, listing
   the gaps, rather than guessing.
3. **Never a secret.** No card number, CVV, expiry, PIN, password or OTP, and no whole bank
   or loan account number — the last four digits are fine. The validator refuses a save
   carrying a card number or a credential, and names the row. A number of 13 to 19 digits
   can read as a card number and be refused: write its last four digits, and name the
   document that holds it in full. Dates in notes are written YYYY-MM-DD, never 03/27,
   which can read as a card's expiry.
4. **The present, not a log.** When the commitment changes — its price, its cycle, its
   member, what you learned about it — rewrite the note so it describes the commitment as
   it now stands. Never append "updated on…" lines: the Proposals screen keeps every version,
   and `_provenance` keeps who wrote what and from where.
5. **A document is named, never pasted** — by its path in `documents/`.

A charge's own `note` stays a word about that one charge. `details` on a commitment is
longbook's own — `statement_line`, the words a statement printed, written when longbook
reads a statement itself: read it, never write it.

An account's `notes` hold its details the same way, one per line as `Label: value` — on a
card, "Card name: Platinum Reserve", the product printed on it, never its number. A member
has no notes: a name, a tag, an email and linked accounts are all it carries.

A truer start is a question for the owner, not a decision: "this insurance has run since
2018" when the file's first row is 2024 means the earlier premiums were paid — the only
question is whether the owner wants those years in his memory. Ask. If yes, `add_charges`
with `paid: true`, at the year's premium where a document says it and at today's otherwise,
noting which. "Since" is the earliest row, so writing them moves it.

Where your own reference belongs: `_provenance.source` for where a write came from
(`"gmail:18c2…"`, `"documents/hdfc-2026.pdf"`), a charge's own `note` for a word about
that one charge. A commitment's notes hold its details, never your bookkeeping. Everything
you keep is in the file the owner reads.

## Reading reports — drawn by longbook, read by you

longbook draws one report for every calendar month holding a **confirmed** charge, into
`reports/<month>-<year>.json` — `july-2026.json`, `june-2026.json` — and redraws it when the
month's rows change. It also draws spans of days: a trip the owner adds in the app, and any
span asked for with `create_report` — redrawn with the months, on the same rules.

A charge is confirmed when it is dated today or earlier and its `basis` is anything but
`"plan"` — a statement, a mail, the owner's word, the app's own paid-tap. A row with no
`basis` reads as `"plan"`, as it does everywhere else. **That one rule decides both things:
which months are drawn, and what each report counts.** A month holding nothing but the plan
draws no report, because a report of it would describe a month nobody has confirmed; the
month ahead never draws; and a transfer confirms nothing. No statement is needed — charges
the owner typed draw their month like any other.

**A report counts confirmed charges only**, in every figure it holds: the total, the count,
"Money in", both rings, the charge list, and the month it is compared against. So a month
part-way confirmed reports the part that is confirmed and no more — a report is what moved,
not what is expected to. The rest of the month is still on the timeline and in the
dashboard's own figures, which do count a past row whatever its basis; a report is the one
surface that will not.

**And it says when it is short**, so you never read a light month as a cheap one. A month is
**part-covered** when a charge in it, in the report's own currency, has passed and is not
confirmed. Then, and only then, the stats carry a **"Not yet confirmed"** stat with the count of
those charges — the "Total expenses" figure is what longbook can account for, and that stat says
how many charges it could not.

Coverage is measured in the report's own currency, because that is what its figures are in. A
dollar row nobody has confirmed does not make a rupee report part-covered; the dollar month is
its own report, with its own coverage.

**`delta_pct` and `delta_is_good` are absent** whenever a change cannot honestly be drawn,
which is any of three things. Read absence as "longbook would not say", never as a month of
no spending, and never compute the change yourself from two reports:

1. **The month is not over.** The current month's report covers its passed days only, so it
   never carries a change: five days of September against the whole of August is a fall of
   98% that did not happen. A month gets its change the first time it is drawn after it ends.
2. **Either month is part-covered.** A whole month against a short one reports missing
   evidence as thrift, and `delta_is_good` would call it good news.
3. **The month before holds no confirmed spending in this currency** — the vault's earliest
   month, or a month whose spending was all in some other currency. There is nothing to
   compare with, which is not the same as nothing having been spent.

Say what the stats say. A report carrying "Not yet confirmed" is the month as far as longbook
knows it, and the way to make it the whole month is to reconcile the month — a statement, the
mail, or the owner marking what they recognise — after which that stat goes and, once the month
is over, a change appears. Never present a part-covered figure as the month's spending, and
never fill the gap with an estimate of your own.

longbook still draws every report, and a file you put in that folder is not what the app
draws. `create_report` is how an AI asks it to draw one — over days, accounts, people or
categories the owner chooses ("create-a-report"). What you do with a report is read it, say
what it shows, and — when the owner wants it different — change the rows behind it, so the
next draw says the true thing.

`reports` is the tool. With no id it lists what is there, newest first by the last day each
covers: the title, its `start_date` and `end_date`, its `scope`, the month when it is one,
the day the file was written, how many modules and how many comments each holds, and the
share link when one is live. With an id it returns that report whole — every module as the
app draws it, each with its own comments.

A drawn report holds these modules, in this order:

1. **`stats`, "Total expenses"** — the stat "Total expenses" is the month's total, against
   the month before when a change can be drawn (`delta_pct`, `delta_is_good`, and
   `delta_label` naming the month, "vs August"); money in another currency is a further
   "Total expenses" stat in that currency, never blended in; "Charges" counts every row the
   list holds, whatever its currency; "Not yet confirmed" appears only in a part-covered
   month; "Money in" when the month had any.
2. **`donut`, "Accounts"** — one slice per paying account, biggest first, with "No account"
   among them when charges were billed to none.
3. **`donut`, "Categories"** — one slice per tag, biggest first, "No category" among them.
4. **`transactions`, "All charges"** — every confirmed charge in the month, biggest first,
   uncapped. A row names its charge (`id`), its `account` and its `member` when it has
   them. A row the owner took out of the report carries `removed: true`, is listed last, and
   is in no figure; a charge dropped for good is named in the envelope's `hidden_ids` and
   listed nowhere.

The total and the charge list are always drawn. Both rings are drawn from the report's own
currency, so a month holding no charge in that currency holds neither ring: a drawn report is
one, two or four modules, never three.

Only the report's own currency enters a ring; a slice in any other is listed beside it with
its own sum and no share. An `Accounts` slice is an account name the owner typed and is shown
exactly as typed; a `Categories` slice is a tag, and a screen shows it with a capital.

The envelope: `version` 2, `id` (the filename), `title` ("July 2026", or the name the owner
gave — "Goa"), `subtitle` ("Drawn by longbook"), `start_date` and `end_date` (the days it
covers), `period` (`"2026-07"` only when it is one calendar month), `scope` (the `accounts`,
`members` and `categories` it was narrowed to, lists that must all match; absent means all of
them, "No account" stands for charges billed to no account and "No category" for untagged
ones), `hidden_ids`, `created_at` (the day the file was written, never the days it covers),
`currency`, `modules`. A month's id is `<month>-<year>`.

A report over any other span of days has the same shape, with its own `start_date`,
`end_date` and `scope`, and no `period`. A **trip**'s id is `trip-` with its name and first
day — `trip-goa-2026-09-28`; a span asked for with `create_report` is named `report-` the
same way — `report-school-fees-2026-07-01`. When a report with other days or another scope already
holds that id, the new one takes `-2`, then `-3`; the same name, days and scope again redraws
the same file. longbook redraws both from their own name, days and scope whenever it redraws
the months. A trip still running — started with "Start trip mode" and not yet ended with "End
trip" — is named in `longbook.workspace.json` (`openTrip`, longbook's own), and its `end_date`
moves to today at each redraw until it ends. A span's `currency` is the one most of its
confirmed charges are in, else the home currency. The listing's order is the Reports
screen's: the newest last covered day first, then the newer file, then the filename; a
report naming no days lists last.

A file older than this version may hold other module kinds — `prose`, `bars`, or a kind this
text does not name. They still read, and `reports` returns them as they are.

### Comments

Every module carries a `comment`: the owner's own line, and the lines pulled back from a
shared link when they shared the report with someone. `reports` returns them per module, one
string per line, in the words they were written in. Quote them; never rewrite them, never
summarise them into something the writer did not say. They are the one part of a report
nobody drew.

### What the owner asks for, and what to do

- *"What did I spend in July in my longbook?"* — `reports` with the month, and read the "Total expenses"
  module back. The figures are drawn from the rows; quote them, never recompute them.
- *"Why is July so high?"* — the "All charges" module is the month, biggest first. Name the
  charges that made it, not a share of a total.
- *"This category is wrong"* / *"that charge was for my mother"* — that is the month's data,
  not the report. Fix the row — `update_commitment`, `add_charges`, `remove_charges`,
  `update_account`, `update_person` — and say the report redraws itself from it.
- *"What did Meera say?"* — the comments on the module she left them on.
- *"Make a report of my Goa trip in my longbook"* — the prompt `Make a report of my trip`, built on
  "create-a-report": ask for its days, accounts and people, then one `create_report`.

A report is never edited into agreement with the owner. The rows are the memory; the report
is what the rows come to.

## Month report — adding the month the owner names

"Add September month report in my longbook" asks for September made whole, so that longbook
draws it: you write no report, and `reports` only reads. Say where you are in time first —
the month named, and today. Then `charges` from the month's first day to its last (and
`reports` on the Mac, when the month is already drawn) for what is there and on what
basis: a passed row whose basis is "plan" is unconfirmed, and it is what puts a "Not yet
confirmed" stat beside the report's "Total expenses".

Ask which bank and card statements cover the month: on the Mac, `list_documents` names
what is in `documents/`; through a hosted door, ask the owner to attach them. Import them
by "importing-statements" — every line a one-time row at its real date and amount, paid,
basis "statement". A row already there that the statement proves is `add_charges` on it,
paid, basis "statement", never a twin; a charge the month held only as a plan is confirmed
the same way. Each statement's closing balance goes on its account — `update_account` with
`balance` and `balance_date` the statement's last day — so the Accounts module shows the
month's end rather than an older day; skip it when the statement prints none. Then say it: longbook draws the report the next time the app applies the
change, with a "Not yet confirmed" stat beside "Total expenses" until every passed charge in
the month is confirmed, and without it after.

## Create a report — any days, narrowed to accounts, members or categories

"Create a report in my longbook" asks longbook to draw a report over days the owner chooses —
a trip, a quarter, one person's spending, one card's month. longbook draws it from the
ledger: you write no report, and you never compute or state its figures yourself.

Before you call anything, ask the owner, in one message:

1. **The name** — what the report is called on the Reports screen ("Goa", "Q3 household").
2. **The first and last day.** The first is today or earlier; 366 days at most, both counted.
3. **Which accounts and which people.** Choosing nobody means everyone.
4. **Categories** — only if they want to narrow by them.

Then read `accounts`, `people` and `tags` for the real names, and pass each as the memory
holds it. "No account" means charges billed to no account and "No category" untagged ones;
any other name the memory does not hold is refused with the real names, and nothing is ever
created to fit.

Make ONE `create_report` call — `title`, `start_date`, `end_date`, and `accounts`,
`members` or `categories` only where the owner narrowed it; on a hosted door, with an
`idempotency_key`. Then say that longbook draws it on its Reports screen the next time the
app is open, counting confirmed charges only as every report does, and stop. Nothing waits in
Proposals. The same name, days and scope asked again redraws the same report, so a retry is
harmless.

To change what it says, fix the rows — the charge and commitment tools — and longbook redraws
it. Other days or another scope is another report. Once drawn, `reports` reads it on the Mac.
With only the folder there is no way to ask: `requests/` is longbook's own, never written by
hand.

A trip is the same kind of report. The owner can also add one in the app, under Settings →
Trips on the Mac or More → Trips on iPhone, and start trip mode for one still running.

## Leaving insights

Beside the ledger you can keep `insights.json` — short notes about what the numbers cannot
say, shown inside the app on the module each note belongs to. `leave_insight` appends one;
by hand the shape is:
