`{ "version": 1, "insights": [ { "module": "dashboard.this_month", "text": "August runs over
July — the travel booking, not a trend.", "created_at": "2026-08-07" } ] }`

Append new entries rather than editing old ones; the last entry for a module wins. Module
ids: `dashboard.next_payment`, `dashboard.active_commitments`, `dashboard.next_30_days`,
`dashboard.this_month`, `dashboard.by_account`, `dashboard.by_category`, plus
`account.<account_id>` and `member.<member_id>` for one account or person. Say what the
numbers cannot; never repeat them. Quote the owner's names exactly as typed. An id from a
newer contract than the app is kept for the version that names it — it is not an error.

**There are no `reports.*` ids.** The Reports screen shows the months longbook drew and
nothing else, so `reports.summary`, `reports.cash_flow`, `reports.spendings`,
`reports.by_account` and `reports.top_charges` name screens that are not there; a note
written on one has nowhere to appear, and longbook says so instead of hiding it. What you
would have said about a month belongs in the conversation, or on the dashboard module it is
about. Notes already written against those ids stay in `insights.json` exactly as they
were; longbook does not edit the owner's file to tidy its own vocabulary.

## Unattended runs — when no one is watching

An AI that runs on a schedule (a morning brief, a receipts sweep, a renewal watch) writes
into longbook without the owner in the conversation. The rules above still hold; these are
added because nobody is there to catch a mistake:

- **Call `whoami` first, every run.** One call tells you who the connection belongs to,
  what it may do, what is left of the rate allowance, whether a hosted copy exists, how many
  proposals are waiting for the owner, how many FAILED to apply, and the vault's real tag
  names. If it says `can_write: false`, read `how_to_enable`, and say that sentence to the
  owner rather than trying anyway. `failed_to_apply` lists the newest suggestions the app
  could not carry out (up to 20; `failed_to_apply_count` is the total), each with its
  reason — usually a name the memory does not hold. Fix the cause with the real names and
  file again under the same `idempotency_key`, so the corrected proposal replaces the
  failed one; never resend the same payload.
- **Both doors write; they land differently.** On the owner's own machine the local server
  writes the file, and the batch appears in Proposals at once. From the cloud — either signed
  in as the owner, or carrying a key with `memory:propose` — a write is a **proposal**:
  nothing out there touches the memory, and the owner's app applies it, on their Mac or
  their iPhone, whichever they open next, where it stands in Proposals to keep or undo like
  any other outside edit. `write_mode` in whoami says which door you are at. The honest
  sentence to the owner is "it will be waiting in Proposals the next time you open longbook",
  never "done".
- **If the write tools refuse with `insufficient_scope`, read `how_to_enable` and say it.**
  Suggestions from a signed-in AI are off until the owner turns them on ("Let signed-in AIs
  suggest changes", on the app's Automations screen); a key needs "Read and suggest changes".
  The tools are listed either way, so you can always tell the owner exactly what to switch on.
- **Idempotency is yours to keep, and the door helps.** Send an `idempotency_key` on every
  hosted write, built from the SOURCE and the WRITE — not from the date:
  `{source id}:{tool}:{short hash of the payload}`, e.g. `18c2a:add_commitments:9f3c1d`.
  A date in the key is wrong in both directions: two writes drawn from one email collide
  inside a single run and the second is silently swallowed, and tomorrow's date makes a
  fresh key for the same email, filing a real duplicate. A repeat answers
  `created: false` with the same entry id: that is success, not an error; do not send it
  again a third way. The promise holds for ninety days — a suggestion is deleted ninety
  days after it was filed, and a key that old files afresh. Where no source id exists, `search` for the name and check `notes`
  and `_provenance.source` before adding.
- **Cite the source on every write**: pass `source` (`"gmail:18c2…"`,
  `"documents/icici-aug.pdf"`). It becomes `_provenance.source`, and the owner reads it in
  the diff beside your key's name.
- **Read the error code, not the sentence.** Every refusal carries one: `rate_limited`
  (wait `retry_after` seconds, then continue), `validation_failed` (fix that row or drop
  it — never retry the same payload), `insufficient_scope` / `key_revoked` / `key_expired`
  / `entitlement_required` (stop and tell the owner; nothing you retry will help — the hosted
  copy needs longbook Cloud, and on a Mac the same work is free through the local server),
  `conflict` or `upstream_error` (try once more later). `advice` says "retry" or "stop"
  in as many words.
- **One batch, one report, silence.** Write once, leave a short `leave_insight` if it
  helps, and end. Never loop write-check-rewrite.
- **Tell the owner, never decide for them.** An unattended run adds `once` rows and
  proposes promotions in its note; it does not cancel, does not promote, does not change
  amounts on its own authority unless the source is a price-change notice from the payee
  itself. The one plan it extends: when it marks a charge paid and no charge is written
  after it, it writes the next one — one cycle on, `add_charges` at the commitment's
  price — so the commitment keeps a next due. Say so in the report.
- **The key lives in a credential store, never in a file or the prompt.** On a Mac the app
  offers "Save to keychain" the one time the key is shown; a run on that machine then reads
  it without the key ever touching disk:
  `security find-generic-password -s "longbook access key" -w`
  (the first read asks once — choose Always Allow). Hand it to an MCP config through the
  environment, not by pasting: `export LONGBOOK_KEY="$(security find-generic-password -s
  'longbook access key' -w)"` and then `"Authorization": "Bearer ${LONGBOOK_KEY}"` in the
  connector config. In a cloud scheduler, use its own secret store the same way. Keys are
  named, scoped and revoked on the app's Automations screen; a revoked key stops at once,
  and an expiring one is reported by `whoami` before it bites.

A morning brief, end to end: `whoami` → `upcoming` (30 days) and `next_payment` for the
lines the owner wants read out → for each receipt or notice in the mail: `search` the payee,
then `add_commitments` (or `update_commitment` for a price change, `mark_paid` for a
"payment received", plus the next cycle's charge when the plan ended with it) with `source`
and `idempotency_key` → one `leave_insight` if something is worth saying → report to the
owner what was filed and that it is waiting in Proposals.

## The daily email round — a scheduled look at the owner's mail

The owner may ask you to "set yourself up for a daily longbook email round". It is one
scheduled task: each morning you read the last day of their mail for money that moved, or
is about to, and write what you find into longbook. Everything in "Unattended runs" holds;
this chapter is the method.

**Setting it up, once.**

1. Call `whoami`. If `can_write` is false, say its `how_to_enable` sentence and stop there.
2. Check that you can read the owner's mail. If you cannot, say so: the round needs a mail
   connector.
3. Create a scheduled task that runs every day at 06:00 in the owner's time zone. Its
   instructions: call `read_guide` with "daily-email-round" on the longbook connector, then
   do "Each run" as that chapter says — so every morning reads the method as it stands that
   day. If your app has no scheduled tasks, say so, and offer to run the round whenever the
   owner asks for it.
4. Run the first round now, so the owner sees in Proposals what a morning looks like.

**One month, on request.** "Add email invoices in my longbook" is the same reading, once,
over the calendar month so far — no scheduled task. `whoami`, then steps 2 to 7 of "Each
run", with the search window the month's first day to today, taking the kinds of mail below
as they stand, a bill due ahead included at its due date. Report once and stop.

**Each run.**

1. `whoami` first. Anything under `failed_to_apply` is earlier work that did not land: fix
   it with the real names and file it again under the same `idempotency_key`.
2. Search the mail since the last round — the last 24 hours, or 36 to be safe — for the
   kinds of mail listed below.
3. Read the memory before you write: `accounts` gives every account with its type, its
   notes (a card's name among them), last four digits and next unpaid charge, and
   `people` every person with their tag; `commitments` gives what still lies ahead with
   its price, cycle, category, account and person; `charges` with `from` set to the
   first day you are looking back over gives what is already written, card bills among
   them. A mail whose amount and day are already there was written by an earlier round, or
   by a bank message: skip it. This look is what stops a twin; an idempotency key only
   protects a retry of the same call.
4. The fields longbook takes are in each write tool's input schema and in the chapter
   "shape": a name, an amount with its currency, a date, `billing_cycle`, `paid`, `basis`,
   `direction` for money in and for a transfer, and, when the mail says so, a category, an
   `account`, a `member` and a short note.
5. From each mail draw exactly those. The amount and its currency. The day the money moved,
   which is not always the day the mail arrived. Who it went to or came from, as a plain
   name: "Corner Grocery", never the payment handle, never "UPI transfer". The account in
   the memory whose name carries the last four digits the mail shows. A category from
   `tags`, the library's before a new one. A person only when the memory holds them.
6. Write each mail once, in a call of its own, so it carries its own
   `source: "gmail:<message id>"` and an `idempotency_key` built from that id. `search` the
   payee first. Money that belongs to a commitment the memory holds goes on it with
   `add_charges`: the open charge's own date, `paid: true`, the amount, `paid_on` and
   `basis: "email"` — a row already there for that day is updated in place — and a new date
   only when no charge is open. Anything else is an `add_commitments` row of its own,
   `basis: "email"`, paid or unpaid as its kind below says.
7. End with one short report: how many rows, which mails you skipped and why in a line,
   what needs the owner's word (a row that looks recurring, an account the memory does not
   hold), and that it is waiting in Proposals. Then stop.

**The kinds of mail, and what each becomes.**

- **A bank's debit alert** — UPI, card, net banking: "Rs.250.00 is debited from your account
  ending 1234 towards VPA shop@bank (SHOP NAME) on 05-08-26". A charge: a one-time row at
  its real date and amount, paid. The name is the shop or person the mail names, the words
  in brackets after the handle. When the payee is a commitment the memory holds — a
  subscription, a premium, a salary the owner pays — the alert is that commitment's charge,
  never a twin beside it.
- **A card alert** — "Thank you for using your Debit Card ending 1234 for Rs. 1,499.00 at
  MERCHANT on 07-08-2026". The same.
- **An autopay or e-mandate chain** — a consent request with an OTP, "consent received",
  "deducted from your account", "successfully paid": four mails, one payment. Write it
  once, from the mail that says the money left. A consent request, an OTP and a pre-debit
  notice are not charges; when a pre-debit notice names a new amount for a commitment the
  memory holds, say so in the report.
- **A receipt or an invoice from the seller** — a subscription receipt, a service invoice,
  a ride, a food order. Usually the same money a bank alert already reported: match on the
  amount and the day, write it once, and let the receipt give the better name, the category
  and the note. A receipt paid in cash has no bank alert and is a charge of its own.
- **A bill that is due** — "payment is due for your service, amount 1,800.00". When the
  memory holds the commitment, the bill is its next charge: check that charge's date and
  amount, and add nothing. When it does not, a one-time row, `paid: false`, at its due date;
  when its payment shows in a later round, that row is the one to mark paid.
- **Money in** — salary, a refund, interest, cashback, a dividend, once the bank says it was
  credited: a one-time row with `direction: "in"`, paid. A notice that a refund is on its
  way is not the credit.
- **An insurance or renewal notice** — when the memory holds the commitment, check its next
  charge's date and amount against the notice; correct the charge only when the notice comes
  from the payee itself, and otherwise say what differs in your report. When the memory does
  not hold the commitment, add a one-time row, unpaid, at the due date, and propose the cycle
  in your report.
- **A credit card statement is ready** — ONE one-time row named for the card and the month
  it falls due, "<Card> bill, <month> <year>" ("Coral card bill, October 2026"),
  `direction: "transfer"`, `paid: false`, at the due date, the amount the total due,
  `account` the card when the memory holds it, `basis: "email"`. The month is in the name
  because a card has a bill every month: each is its own row, and a name two rows share
  cannot address either. Never spending: every spend on that card is a charge already, and
  the bill that pays them is a movement between the owner's own accounts — a transfer is
  shown and counted in nothing. A bill already written for that month is corrected in
  place, never doubled. Import the statement's own lines, by "importing-statements", only
  when the owner has asked for card statements to be imported.
- **A card bill payment** — it settles the transfer row for that month: find it with
  `search`, and address it by id. `add_charges` on that row, its own date,
  `paid: true`, `paid_on` the day the money moved, the amount paid, `basis: "email"` —
  updated in place. Skip it only when the memory holds no such row.
- **A wallet top-up, a transfer to the owner's own account, an investment bought** —
  movements. Skip them, unless the memory holds the payment as a commitment of its own — a
  monthly investment plan, a standing transfer — and then it is that commitment's charge.
- **Skip entirely** — OTPs, sign-in alerts, offers and newsletters, brokerage and mutual
  fund statements, margin and portfolio reports, tax intimations, forex mark-up notices
  (the fee arrives as its own debit), and anything that names no amount.

The last four digits of a card or an account are for matching only. Never write a card
number, an account number, an OTP or a tax id anywhere.

## The shape

- `app` — `"longbook"`.
- `version` — the file format, currently 3. Not a revision counter; leave it alone.
- `commitments[]` — the only required list, and only what every charge shares: name,
  amount (the price now), currency, billing_cycle (monthly | yearly | custom | once — shown
  as Commitment Type), status, free_trial (true while the owner marks it one), tag, notes
  (its three details that matter), details (longbook's own statement line — read, never
  written), ends_on, direction (in | out | transfer — only "out", or none, is spending),
  and two foreign keys: member_id,
  account_id. Nothing about an occurrence lives here.
- `charges[]` — every charge, past and planned, one row per commitment per due date:
  commitment_id, date, amount, paid, and optionally currency, paid_on, basis (statement |
  user | mark_paid | plan | email), note, written_at. The only place an occurrence exists.
- `members[]`, `accounts[]` — who a commitment is for, and what it is billed to. The `people`
  tool lists the first; the file keeps its older key. Both carry
  a tag, details — longbook's own, read as stored, never written — and starred (true when
  the owner starred one to keep it first; set it only when they ask); an account also notes
  (its details, one per line, a card's name among them), member_id (the person it belongs
  to) and parent_account_id (its linked account).
- `tags[]` — the vocabulary: kind (commitment | member | account), name and icon. No tag
  carries a template.
- `groups[]` — optional; the owner's own labels over what already exists, never new records.
  An "account" group lists account_ids, a "member" group member_ids, a "tag" group tag_keys —
  one named "business" holding tag_keys groups those tags wherever longbook totals spending.
  A tag belongs to at most one group; anything ungrouped is simply ungrouped, not "other".
- `to_fill_in[]` — optional; commitments the owner named at setup or ticked from a
  statement, and nobody has filled in: id, name, group, tag. Not commitments. Find each
  one's amount and day, write it with `add_commitments` under the same name, and the entry
  goes; ask the owner for what you cannot find.
- `hints[]` — optional; people and accounts the owner picked at setup by role or kind: id,
  name, kind (member | account), tag. Not members or accounts, and nothing points at one. Read
  statements with them in mind; add the person or account under the name a statement or the
  owner gives, and leave the hint alone.
- `_provenance` — optional map keyed by record id: who last edited it, when, from what source.
  longbook adds `reviewed_by`/`reviewed_at` when the owner keeps your change and keeps an
  entry for a row it removed; leave both alone and replace the whole entry when you edit a row.

Neighbours in the folder: `documents/` (statements and source documents — the owner's and
yours to add to), `reports/` (reports, JSON — one per calendar month, named for it, plus
trips and the spans asked for with `create_report`; all drawn by longbook and read with
`reports`), `requests/` (longbook's own: what an AI asked of it through `create_report` on
this machine, waiting for the app, which carries each out and removes it — never write or
edit it by hand),
`insights.json` (your notes), `library.json` (the tag library this text lists),
`longbook.schema.json` (the formal schema),
`longbook.workspace.json` (display preferences — longbook's own, never edit) and
`.longbook/` (change history — never edit; editing history would defeat the owner's ability
to review and undo changes, yours included).

## The past is evidence

A charge row is the truth about one occurrence, and `basis` says what backs it. Best
first: `"statement"` and `"email"` — a document says so; `"user"` — the owner said so,
or priced it by hand; `"mark_paid"` — the app's own paid-tap; `"plan"` — written ahead
at the commitment's price, confirmed by nobody yet. Anything but `"plan"` is a fact, and
nothing reprices a fact.

- The owner's word is the starting point, not the last word. Write what they tell you with
  `basis: "user"`.
- A document is better evidence. When a bank statement or an email arrives, reconcile against
  it: correct the amount AND the date (`paid_on`), set `basis: "statement"` or `"email"`,
  and point `_provenance.source` at the document in `documents/`. `add_charges` does this
  on a row that exists — a row already there for that day is updated in place; a row that
  does not is written. `mark_paid` carries no basis, so it is for the owner's word alone.
- Never replace a statement- or email-backed figure with the owner's recollection. Evidence
  does not degrade.
- One row per occurrence, ever. Correcting is not a second row beside the first: change the
  row that exists and let `basis` say where the number now comes from.
- `basis: "mark_paid"` is longbook's own paid-tap. Never write it yourselves.
- A row that has passed and is still `"plan"` is unconfirmed, not wrong. Leave it, mark it
  when the owner says it was paid, or correct it when a statement arrives.

The future is the plan as written, and only as far as it was written. Never write a charge
you were not asked for, and never remove a paid one without saying so.

## Invariants

- Foreign keys must resolve — a dangling member_id or account_id blocks the save.
- Amounts are finite and non-negative; dates are real calendar dates.
- `name_key` (trimmed + lowercased name) is the dedup key for members, accounts and tags.
- Details values are scalars or flat lists — never nested objects.
- `custom_cycle_days` only with `billing_cycle: "custom"`. One charge per commitment
  per date. A one-time commitment has exactly one.
- An invalid file on disk is preserved and reported, never silently overwritten.

## Rules for anything that writes

1. Preserve ids — they are UUIDs and they are load-bearing.
2. Never convert or blend currencies. Totals are per-currency, always.
3. Never write a charge nobody asked for; plan as far as the owner said, and say how far.
4. Sign your work in _provenance; cite the document a row came from.
5. Prefer cancelling over deleting — a cancelled commitment keeps every charge that
   happened and drops only the plan ahead. `delete_commitment` removes a commitment and
   every charge it ever had, and is for the owner's own sentence "delete it", never for
   tidying.
6. Never write a full card number, CVV, expiry, PIN, or credential anywhere in this file.
7. Keep source documents in documents/ and reference them; never paste their contents.
8. Dedupe before adding; once when in doubt; one batch, then stop for review.
   Names are read on one-line cards: a commitment's name is whole up to about 28
   characters, an account's or a person's up to about 20, and a longer one is cut with an
   ellipsis on the phone. Write names the owner would say, short enough to be read whole.
9. longbook drops a malformed entry alone — a charge that fails the schema vanishes from
   every screen while the rest of the vault keeps working. If something you wrote is not
   showing up, do not rewrite it blind: validate this file against `longbook.schema.json`
   and check the vault's shape first.
10. Read before you write. Every `read_guide` answer carries a `guide_key`, and so does a
   prompt's own message; pass it with every write the procedure makes. A write without one,
   or with one from another rulebook, is answered with a `guide_warning` naming what to
   read; from the next rulebook it is refused. Charges with basis "statement" take the key
   of `importing-statements`, or of a prompt built on it.

The formal schema: `longbook.schema.json`, right beside this file. The seeded tag library
with icons: `library.json`, beside it too. Both are served by the longbook MCP servers as
resources, and `read_guide` returns any chapter of this text by name. The owner's prompts:
`prompts.json`, beside them, the same list the `Prompts` chapter holds.
